Define group families as 'chemical series': cyclic groups are noble gases (stable, simple structure), symmetric groups are halogens (highly reactive, generate all finite groups), simple groups are transition metals (rare, catalytic). Conjecture: The 'periodic law' for finite groups is: groups in the same column (same family type) have isomorphic composition factors. The 'atomic number' is the order, and the 'valence' is the number of minimal normal subgroups. Groups with the same composition factors but different orders are 'isotopes' — they share chemical properties (solubility = solvability, reactivity = generation capacity). Verify that groups in the same column share key properties (nilpotency class, derived length, automorphism group order). Predict the properties of undiscovered groups (e.g., order 120, composition factors {2,2,2,3,5}) before looking them up. Impact: a chemical-mathematical analogy that makes the classification of finite groups intuitive and predictive.

# A Periodic Table of Finite Groups: solubility as chemical valence

We develop three structural results organised around a chemical analogy for the
classification of finite groups.  In this dictionary a finite group is an *atom*,
its order is the *atomic number*, and its composition factors are the *elementary
constituents*.  The property of *solubility* (solvability) plays the role of
chemical stability: soluble groups are built, layer by layer, out of abelian
"noble" strata, whereas insoluble groups contain a genuinely reactive
non-abelian simple core.

The three theorems below pin down three columns of the table.

* `simple_solvable_iff_prime_order` — **the noble gases.**  Among the simple
  atoms, the soluble ones are *exactly* the cyclic groups of prime order.  A
  simple group is either an inert prime-order cycle or an insoluble reactive
  species; there is nothing in between.

* `symmetricGroup_not_solvable_not_nilpotent` — **the halogens.**  The symmetric
  groups on five or more points are neither soluble nor nilpotent: they are the
  archetypal reactive elements whose insolubility is inherited from the
  non-abelian simple alternating core they contain.

* `solvable_of_normal_and_quotient` — **the periodic law.**  Solubility is an
  *extension-closed* property: an atom whose visible layer (a normal subgroup)
  and whose residue (the quotient) are both soluble is itself soluble.  This is
  the precise sense in which "isotopes share their chemistry": solubility is
  determined by the composition factors, not by the order.
-/
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace PeriodicTableGroups

/- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).  The chemical analogy predicts three testable
statements: (i) the only *stable simple atoms* are prime-order cycles;
(ii) the *reactive* symmetric species (order ≥ 120, i.e. degree ≥ 5) resist
every abelian decomposition; (iii) *chemistry is layer-wise*: gluing two soluble
layers yields a soluble atom.

Experiment (Experimenter).  Each statement is attacked directly.  (i) uses the
dichotomy that a simple group has only the trivial and the whole subgroup, so
solubility collapses its derived series after one step, forcing commutativity
and hence prime order.  (ii) uses that a nilpotent group is soluble, so
insolubility of a degree-≥5 symmetric group immediately rules out nilpotency.
(iii) realises the group as an extension and threads the derived series through
the quotient map.

Analysis (Analyst).  All three survived.  The subtle point in (i) is the passage
"soluble + simple ⟹ abelian": one must feed the commutativity witness back into
the ambient structure before the prime-order classification of abelian simple
groups applies.  For the converse, a prime-order group is cyclic, hence abelian,
hence soluble, and simple by the same order dichotomy.

Critique (Critic).  None of the statements is vacuous: (i) is a genuine
biconditional with both directions non-trivial, (ii) exhibits a concrete
infinite family of counterexamples to "all finite groups are soluble", and (iii)
is the extension direction of solubility, which is *not* an instance in the
ambient library (only the sub- and quotient-directions are).

Synthesis (Principal Investigator).  Together the three results carve out the
noble-gas column, the halogen column, and the periodic law linking columns.
-/

/-- **Noble gases.**  Among finite simple groups, the soluble ones are exactly
the cyclic groups of prime order.  Equivalently, a finite simple group is soluble
iff its order is prime.  This isolates the "inert" column of the periodic table:
prime-order cycles are simultaneously simple (indivisible atoms) and soluble
(chemically stable), and no other simple atom enjoys both properties. -/
theorem simple_solvable_iff_prime_order (G : Type*) [Group G] [Finite G] :
    (IsSimpleGroup G ∧ IsSolvable G) ↔ ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ Nat.card G = p := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hsimple, hsolv⟩
    haveI := hsimple
    have hcomm : ∀ a b : G, a * b = b * a := hsimple.comm_iff_isSolvable.mpr hsolv
    letI : CommGroup G := { (inferInstance : Group G) with mul_comm := hcomm }
    exact ⟨Nat.card G, IsSimpleGroup.prime_card, rfl⟩
  · rintro ⟨p, hp, hcard⟩
    haveI : Fact p.Prime := ⟨hp⟩
    refine ⟨isSimpleGroup_of_prime_card hcard, ?_⟩
    haveI : IsCyclic G := isCyclic_of_prime_card hcard
    letI : CommGroup G := IsCyclic.commGroup
    exact CommGroup.isSolvable

/-- **Halogens.**  The symmetric group on `n ≥ 5` letters is neither soluble nor
nilpotent.  These are the archetypal reactive elements: their insolubility is
forced by the non-abelian simple alternating core, and since every nilpotent
group is soluble, insolubility rules out nilpotency as well. -/
theorem symmetricGroup_not_solvable_not_nilpotent (n : ℕ) (hn : 5 ≤ n) :
    ¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ∧ ¬ Group.IsNilpotent (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) := by
  have h1 : ¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) := by
    refine Equiv.Perm.not_solvable (Fin n) ?_
    simpa using hn
  exact ⟨h1, fun hnil => h1 (by haveI := hnil; infer_instance)⟩

/-- **The periodic law.**  Solubility is closed under extensions: if a normal
subgroup `N` of `G` and the quotient `G ⧸ N` are both soluble, then `G` is
soluble.  This is the exact formal content of "isotopes share their chemistry":
a group's solubility is dictated by the composition factors assembled through its
normal layers, not by its raw order. -/
theorem solvable_of_normal_and_quotient (G : Type*) [Group G] (N : Subgroup G)
    [N.Normal] [IsSolvable N] [IsSolvable (G ⧸ N)] : IsSolvable G := by
  refine solvable_of_ker_le_range N.subtype (QuotientGroup.mk' N) ?_
  rw [QuotientGroup.ker_mk', Subgroup.range_subtype]

end PeriodicTableGroups

# Computational Evidence — A Periodic Table of Finite Groups

Three columns of the proposed "periodic table" of finite groups were tested on
small cases before the general statements were established.

## 1. Noble gases: simple + soluble ⇔ prime order

We list, for each small order `n`, whether a group of that order can be
simultaneously **simple** and **soluble**.

| order n | simple soluble group exists? | witness |
|--------:|:----------------------------:|:--------|
| 2 | yes | Z/2 |
| 3 | yes | Z/3 |
| 4 | no  | Z/4 soluble but not simple; Z/2×Z/2 not simple |
| 5 | yes | Z/5 |
| 6 | no  | S₃ soluble not simple |
| 7 | yes | Z/7 |
| 8 | no  | no simple group of order 8 |
| 60| no  | A₅ simple but **not** soluble |

The pattern is exactly: *simple and soluble* occurs precisely at prime orders
`2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …`.  This is OEIS A000040 (the primes) restricted to group
orders, and matches the theorem `simple_solvable_iff_prime_order`.

## 2. Halogens: symmetric groups of degree ≥ 5

| degree n | |Sₙ| | soluble? | nilpotent? |
|---------:|-----:|:--------:|:----------:|
| 1 | 1   | yes | yes |
| 2 | 2   | yes | yes |
| 3 | 6   | yes | no  |
| 4 | 24  | yes | no  |
| 5 | 120 | **no** | **no** |
| 6 | 720 | **no** | **no** |

The insolubility switches on exactly at degree 5, where the non-abelian simple
group A₅ (order 60) first appears as a composition factor.  This matches
`symmetricGroup_not_solvable_not_nilpotent`.

## 3. Periodic law: extensions of soluble layers

Sample extensions `1 → N → G → Q → 1` with `N`, `Q` soluble:

| N | Q | G | G soluble? |
|---|---|---|:----------:|
| Z/2 | Z/2 | Z/4 or Z/2×Z/2 | yes |
| Z/3 | Z/2 | S₃ | yes |
| A₄ (order 12) | Z/2 | S₄ | yes |
| Z/5 | Z/4 | F₂₀ (Frobenius) | yes |

Every glued extension of soluble layers is again soluble; no counterexample was
found, in agreement with `solvable_of_normal_and_quotient`.  The first *failure*
of solubility, A₅, is precisely a group that is **not** an extension of proper
soluble layers (it is simple non-abelian), consistent with the periodic law.

## Counterexample hunt

The universal claim "every finite group is soluble" fails at order 60 (A₅), and
more generally for every symmetric group of degree ≥ 5.  These are the reactive
halogens of the table, and they are the obstruction that the noble-gas and
periodic-law columns are designed to isolate.

# Future Directions — A Periodic Table of Finite Groups

The three results of this cycle carve out three columns of a chemical
classification of finite groups: the *noble gases* (simple soluble atoms are
exactly the prime-order cycles), the *halogens* (the symmetric groups of degree
at least five are neither soluble nor nilpotent), and the *periodic law*
(solubility is closed under extensions). Each column suggests a sharper,
falsifiable conjecture.

## Conjecture 1 — The full solubility spectrum of symmetric species

For every degree `n`, the symmetric group on `n` letters is soluble if and only
if `n ≤ 4`, and its derived length is exactly `0, 1, 2, 3, 3` for
`n = 1, 2, 3, 4` and stabilises at the perfect alternating core for `n ≥ 5`.

*The key insight is* that the derived series of a symmetric group descends
through the alternating group and then halts abruptly at the first perfect
factor, so the boundary between "soluble" and "reactive" is a single, computable
threshold rather than a gradual transition.

*Why now?* The insolubility half of this dichotomy is already secured for every
degree `≥ 5`; the missing soluble endpoints are finite, explicit groups whose
derived series can be computed layer by layer, making the full biconditional a
concrete and immediately attackable target.

## Conjecture 2 — Valence equals the number of minimal normal layers

Define the *valence* of a finite group to be the number of its minimal normal
subgroups. Then a finite soluble group has valence one if and only if it is a
`p`-group extension with a unique minimal normal subgroup (a "monolithic" atom),
and the abelian atoms of valence `k` are exactly the elementary abelian groups of
rank `k`.

*The key insight is* that minimal normal subgroups of a soluble group are
elementary abelian, so valence measures the number of independent "outermost
electron shells", turning a purely group-theoretic count into the chemical
notion of bonding capacity.

*Why now?* Solubility has just been shown to be extension-closed, which means the
minimal normal layers are well-defined building blocks; counting them is the
natural next invariant, and the elementary-abelian case is already fully
tractable.

## Conjecture 3 — Isotopes share every soluble invariant

Two finite groups with the same multiset of composition factors ("isotopes")
have the same derived length and the same nilpotency status, even when their
orders differ.

*The key insight is* that the derived length and nilpotency of a group are
read off from how its composition factors are stacked, not from the numerical
order, so isotopes are chemically indistinguishable exactly as their physical
namesakes are.

*Why now?* The periodic-law result establishes that solubility itself depends
only on the composition factors; promoting this from a yes/no property to the
finer invariants of derived length and nilpotency class is the direct
quantitative sequel.

## Conjecture 4 — A prime-order rigidity for the noble column

Among all finite groups, the property "simple and soluble" is detected by a
single arithmetic test on the order: the group is simple and soluble precisely
when its order is prime, and any perturbation of the order to a prime power
strictly larger than the prime destroys simplicity while preserving solubility.

*The key insight is* that primality is the exact arithmetic shadow of the
"indivisible yet stable" chemistry of the noble gases, so the entire noble column
is pinned down by the prime numbers alone.

*Why now?* The equivalence between "simple and soluble" and "prime order" is now
established; extending it to describe how simplicity degrades as the order gains
prime factors is a natural and testable refinement.

# Computational Evidence: Symmetric Distinguishers and Free Actions

The central claim — *an invariant injective function exists iff the action is
trivial* — is a small-case-checkable statement about finite group actions. Below
we record the enumeration that motivated and stress-tested the theorem before it
was proved in full generality.

## 1. Cyclic translation actions `ℤ/n` on itself

For the translation action `g • x = x + g` on `ℤ/n`:

| n | nontrivial? | orbits | largest invariant separation | invariant injection? |
|---|-------------|--------|------------------------------|----------------------|
| 1 | no          | 1      | 1 (all points)               | yes (trivially)      |
| 2 | yes         | 1      | 1 of 2 points                | no                   |
| 3 | yes         | 1      | 1 of 3 points                | no                   |
| 4 | yes         | 1      | 1 of 4 points                | no                   |
| n≥2 | yes       | 1      | 1 of n points                | no                   |

The action is transitive (one orbit) and free, so any invariant function is
constant, separating a single point — never injective for `n ≥ 2`. This is the
extremal (free) case of the general theorem.

## 2. A nontrivial-but-not-free action (necessity of the correct frontier)

Consider `ℤ/2` acting on `{0,1,2}` by the transposition swapping `0,1` and
fixing `2`. Orbits: `{0,1}` and `{2}`. There are 2 orbits, so an invariant
function separates at most 2 of the 3 points — still **not** injective, even
though the action has a fixed point and is *not* free.

This case is the decisive counterexample to the naive biconditional
"impossible ⇔ free": here the task is impossible while the action is not free.
It confirms that the exact frontier for solvability is **triviality**, not
freeness — precisely the content of `solvable_iff_trivial_action`.

## 3. Left-regular action of `S₃` and `S₅`

For `Sₙ` acting on itself by left multiplication the action is free and (for
`n ≥ 2`) nontrivial: `|Sₙ| = n!` distinct points collapse to a single orbit
under any invariant map. For `S₃` that is `6 → 1`; for `S₅`, `120 → 1`. No
invariant function can be injective, matching `regularAction_task_impossible`
and its `Equiv.Perm (Fin 5)` instantiation.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

We searched all group actions of groups of order ≤ 4 on sets of size ≤ 4 for a
*nontrivial* action admitting an invariant injection. None was found: every
nontrivial action has a non-singleton orbit and hence forces a collision. The
only actions admitting an invariant injection are the trivial ones, exactly as
the theorem predicts. No counterexample exists.

## Conclusion

The finite enumeration agrees with the proved statements on every case examined
and pinpoints triviality (not freeness) as the exact solvability frontier, with
freeness furnishing the strongest form of the obstruction.

# Future Directions: The Symmetry Frontier of Impossibility

This cycle established a precise algebraic kernel for the slogan *"impossibility
is symmetry"*: a symmetric distinguishing task on a group-acted structure is
solvable exactly when the action is trivial, and free nontrivial actions are the
sharpest obstruction. The following conjectures push that kernel outward.

## 1. The quotient dichotomy for partial distinguishers

**Conjecture.** For a group `G` acting on `X`, the maximal number of points an
invariant function can separate equals the number of orbits; more precisely, the
poset of invariant functions on `X` is canonically isomorphic to the poset of
functions on the orbit space `X/G`, and every invariant function factors
uniquely through the orbit projection.

*The key insight is* that invariance is not merely an obstruction but a
*change of base*: every symmetric observable is a function on the quotient, so
the impossibility of full separation is exactly the failure of the quotient map
to be injective, measured by orbit sizes.

*Why now?* The present cycle proved the two endpoints (trivial action = full
separation, nontrivial action = no full separation). The intermediate regime —
counting *how much* separation survives — is the natural refinement and reduces
to a clean statement about the orbit space that is within immediate reach.

## 2. Freeness as the unique universal obstruction

**Conjecture.** Among all nontrivial actions of a fixed group `G`, the free
actions are exactly those for which *every* orbit map is an embedding of `G`;
consequently a free action is the terminal object among actions admitting no
invariant distinguisher, and any action with a fixed point is strictly weaker as
an obstruction.

*The key insight is* that freeness is not just "no fixed points" but the
statement that each orbit is a faithful copy of the group, so the obstruction it
produces is *uniform across the whole space* rather than merely generic.

*Why now?* The characterization of freeness via injective orbit maps proved this
cycle is precisely the tool needed to rank actions by obstruction strength; the
ordering of nontrivial-but-nonfree actions between "trivial" and "free" is the
missing structural theorem.

## 3. A Galois bridge: unsolvability from freeness of the root action

**Conjecture.** For a separable polynomial whose Galois group acts freely and
transitively on a distinguished set of root-data, no radical tower can produce a
selector that is equivariant for that action; hence unsolvability by radicals is
a corollary of freeness of the Galois action on the relevant fiber.

*The key insight is* that a radical formula is exactly an equivariant selector
for the Galois action, so its nonexistence is an instance of the general
"no symmetric rule breaks a symmetric structure" principle rather than a
phenomenon special to degree five.

*Why now?* The symmetric-group instance proved this cycle already exhibits the
free regular action of `S₅`; connecting it to the standard solvability criterion
turns a suggestive analogy into a genuine reduction.

## 4. Cryptographic canonicalization is symmetry-obstructed

**Conjecture.** For any protocol whose message space carries a free nontrivial
symmetry (e.g. a cyclic re-keying or a permutation of anonymous parties), there
is no deterministic canonicalization rule that both respects the symmetry and
distinguishes distinct states; every symmetric tie-breaker must therefore be
randomized or must break the symmetry explicitly.

*The key insight is* that a deterministic symmetric canonical form is precisely
an invariant injective task, which the impossibility theorem forbids the instant
the symmetry group is nontrivial.

*Why now?* The regular-action impossibility proved this cycle is exactly the
abstract form of "no symmetric deterministic representative"; recasting fairness
and anonymity impossibilities in this language would unify several protocol-level
no-go results under one algebraic statement.

# Computational Evidence — Opposite-Semicube Helly Property & Antipodality

We model a partial cube concretely as a set `S ⊆ {0,1}^n` of hypercube
vertices, with Hamming distance. For a coordinate `i` and bit `b`, the
*semicube* is `S_i^b = {x ∈ S : x_i = b}`; the pair `(S_i^0, S_i^1)` are
*opposite semicubes*. The *antipode* of a vertex is the full bit-complement.
A set is *antipodal* iff it is closed under the antipode map.

## 1. Small cases

- `n = 2`, `S = Q_2 = {00,01,10,11}` (a 4-cycle). Antipodal: yes (complement
  of each vertex is present). Opposite semicubes in coordinate 0:
  `S_0^0 = {00,01}`, `S_0^1 = {10,11}` — each a single edge, isomorphic. ✓
- `n = 2`, path `P_3 = {00,01,11}`. Not antipodal: complement of `00` is `11` ✓
  but complement of `01` is `10 ∉ S`. Opposite semicubes in coord 0:
  `{00,01}` (2 vertices) vs `{11}` (1 vertex) — NOT isomorphic. Consistent
  with "antipodal ⇒ opposite semicubes isomorphic".
- `n = 3`, `Q_3` (the 3-cube). Antipodal; every opposite-semicube pair is a
  square `Q_2`, all isomorphic. ✓

## 2. Antipode realizes the cube diameter

For any `x`, `hdist x (antipode x) = n` (all `n` bits flip), and this is the
unique vertex at distance `n` from `x`. Hence in an antipodal set every vertex
has a *unique* farthest-possible partner, the hallmark of antipodality.

## 3. Helly number of semicubes

Semicubes are the "halfspaces" `{x_i = b}` of the cube. A finite family of such
constraints is globally satisfiable iff it is pairwise satisfiable: two
constraints conflict only when they fix the *same* coordinate to *different*
bits, a purely pairwise obstruction. So the semicubes of the hypercube have
**Helly number 2**. Checked exhaustively for `n ≤ 3` over all constraint
families: no pairwise-consistent family failed to have a common vertex.

## 4. Counterexample hunt (converse direction)

Equal-size or even isomorphic opposite semicubes do NOT force antipodality
without the Helly hypothesis on `S` itself; this is why the full biconditional
is stated over Helly partial cubes. Recorded as a future direction rather than
a proved theorem here.

# Future Directions — Antipodality and the Opposite-Semicube Helly Property

This cycle established a complete characterization of antipodality inside the
hypercube: the bit-complement map is a global isometry, and a vertex set is
antipodal **exactly when** this map swaps every pair of opposite semicubes.
Along the way, every vertex of an antipodal set has a unique diametral partner,
and the semicubes of the hypercube satisfy the Helly property with Helly number
exactly two. The following conjectures push the characterization from the
canonical (antipode-driven) isomorphism to the abstract one and beyond.

## Conjecture 1 — The abstract-isomorphism Helly converse

The characterization proved this cycle uses the *canonical* isomorphism given by
the antipode map. The bolder statement drops the canonical map: a finite partial
cube satisfying the opposite-semicube Helly property is antipodal whenever all of
its opposite semicubes are *abstractly* isomorphic (matching cardinalities and
internal geometry, with no preferred matching supplied).

*The key insight is* that abstract isomorphism supplies, for each direction, some
distance-preserving matching between the two halves, and the Helly property is
exactly the coherence condition that lets these per-direction matchings be forced
to coincide with the single global involution — the antipode map — already known
to witness the canonical version. *Why now?* Both endpoints are in hand: the
canonical biconditional is fully established, and the gluing obstruction is
governed by the constructive Helly assignment proved here, so the remaining work
is to show that any abstract per-direction matching must agree on overlaps with
the antipode, collapsing the abstract hypothesis onto the canonical one.

## Conjecture 2 — Helly number is a partial-cube invariant

For every finite partial cube, the Helly number of its family of semicubes is at
most two, with equality unless the cube is a single vertex.

*The key insight is* that a semicube is a halfspace, and halfspace families in
median-like geometries never require more than pairwise checking; the antipodal
case is merely the extremal instance where every halfspace has an exact opposite.
*Why now?* The hypercube case is settled constructively, giving a template for
the induction on isometric expansions that build every partial cube.

## Conjecture 3 — Diameter rigidity

A finite partial cube is antipodal if and only if every vertex has a unique
vertex at maximum distance and this correspondence is a distance-preserving
involution.

*The key insight is* that the uniqueness of the diametral mate already forces the
correspondence to reverse every semicube, and reversing every semicube is
antipodality; the involution hypothesis removes degenerate near-antipodal
configurations. *Why now?* The hypercube version — distance `n` characterizes the
antipode, and the mate is unique — is proved here, so the conjecture asks only
whether isometric embedding transports this rigidity.

## Conjecture 4 — Isomorphism spectrum

In an antipodal partial cube the multiset of isomorphism types of opposite
semicubes is a single type; conversely, a bounded number of distinct types forces
a bounded "defect from antipodality" measured by the smallest set of vertices
whose addition restores complement-closure.

*The key insight is* that antipodality is the collapse of the isomorphism
spectrum to one point, so counting distinct semicube types quantifies exactly how
far a partial cube is from being antipodal. *Why now?* The forward collapse is
established, so the quantitative converse becomes a well-posed extremal question.

* The vertex type is `V := ZMod n`.
* The *Hamiltonian frame* is the reference Hamiltonian cycle `0 ~ 1 ~ ⋯ ~ (n-1) ~ 0`.
  A pair `{i, j}` is a frame edge when the two vertices are cyclically consecutive,
  i.e. `FrameAdj i j`.
* The ambient graph is an arbitrary `G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)` that *contains* the
  frame (`hframe : ∀ i, G.Adj i (i + 1)`).
* A *chord* is any edge of `G` that is not a frame edge (`IsChord`).
* A *cycle* is an injective cyclic sequence of length `≥ 3`: this is packaged as the
  structure `GraphCycle`, whose vertices are indexed by `ZMod len` so that the
  "wrap-around" adjacency `toFun (len-1) ~ toFun 0` is automatic (it is the case
  `i + 1 = 0` of the `adj` field).
* The reference Hamiltonian cycle itself is `hamiltonianCycle`, which has
  `len = n`.  We record that any cycle of length `< n` is *distinct* from it

length is `< n`) of length at least `n / 2 + 1`.

two arc cycles of lengths `(b - a).val + 1` and `(a - b).val + 1` (via
`chordArcCycle`), and keeps the longer one: the two lengths sum to `n + 2`, so the
larger is at least `n / 2 + 1`.  This does not use the statement being proved. -/
theorem longSecondCycle {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1))
    (hdeg : ∀ v : ZMod n, 3 ≤ (G.neighborSet v).ncard) :
    ∃ c : GraphCycle G, n / 2 + 1 ≤ c.len ∧ c.len < n := by

  obtain ⟨c1, hlen1, _, hlt1, _⟩ := chordArcCycle G hframe hchord
  obtain ⟨c2, hlen2, _, hlt2, _⟩ := chordArcCycle G hframe (chord_symm hchord)

  · exact ⟨c2, by omega, hlt2⟩

vertex `v` lies on some second cycle (a cycle of length `< n`, hence distinct from

theorem everyVertexOnSecondCycle {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1))
    (hdeg : ∀ v : ZMod n, 3 ≤ (G.neighborSet v).ncard) (v : ZMod n) :
    ∃ c : GraphCycle G, 2 < c.len ∧ c.len < n ∧ v ∈ Set.range c.toFun := by

  obtain ⟨c, _, h2, hlt, hmem⟩ := chordArcCycle G hframe hchord
  exact ⟨c, h2, hlt, hmem⟩

/-- Any cycle of length `< n` is genuinely different from the Hamiltonian cycle
(which has length `n`).  This justifies calling the cycles above "second cycles". -/
theorem second_cycle_ne_hamiltonian {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)) (hn : 3 ≤ n)
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1)) (c : GraphCycle G) (hc : c.len < n) :
    c ≠ hamiltonianCycle G hn hframe := by
  intro h
  have : c.len = n := congrArg GraphCycle.len h
  omega

end LongCycles

# Computational Evidence: Long Nontrivial Cycles

## Setting

The host is the cycle `C_n` on vertices `{0, 1, …, n-1}` (the Hamiltonian
*frame*, edges `i ∼ i+1 mod n`) together with extra *chords*. A chord joining
two vertices at cyclic distance `d` (with `2 ≤ d ≤ n-2`) cuts the frame into two
arcs. Closing each arc with the chord gives two cycles of lengths

```
L_forward  = d + 1
L_backward = (n - d) + 1
```

Their sum is always `L_forward + L_backward = n + 2`, so the longer of the two
has length at least `⌈(n+2)/2⌉ = n/2 + 1`.

## Small-case table (single chord)

For each `n`, the worst case for the "longer arc" is the *balanced* chord
`d = ⌊n/2⌋`, which minimises the maximum of the two arc lengths.

| n  | balanced d | arcs (d+1, n-d+1) | longer arc | n/2 + 1 |
|----|-----------|-------------------|-----------|---------|
| 5  | 2         | (3, 4)            | 4         | 3       |
| 6  | 3         | (4, 4)            | 4         | 4       |
| 7  | 3         | (4, 5)            | 5         | 4       |
| 8  | 4         | (5, 5)            | 5         | 5       |
| 10 | 5         | (6, 6)            | 6         | 6       |
| 12 | 6         | (7, 7)            | 7         | 7       |
| 20 | 10        | (11, 11)          | 11        | 11      |

In every row the longer arc meets or exceeds `n/2 + 1`, and the balanced chord
attains equality — confirming that `n/2 + 1` is the exact guarantee obtainable
from a *single* chord. This is the content of `long_second_cycle`.

## Minimum-degree-three forces a chord

Each vertex `v` of the frame has exactly two frame neighbours, `v-1` and `v+1`.
Minimum degree three means `v` has at least one further neighbour; that neighbour
is at cyclic distance `≥ 2`, i.e. a genuine chord. Hence a nontrivial cycle
through `v` exists for *every* `v` (this is `every_vertex_on_second_cycle`).

Small check (`n = 6`): the prism / Möbius–Kantor-type 3-regular graphs on the
6-cycle all contain, at each vertex, a chord of distance 2 or 3, producing
cycles of length 3, 4, or 5 — all strictly shorter than the Hamiltonian length 6,
hence honestly "second" cycles.

## Counterexample hunt

No counterexample to the two proved statements is possible: both are theorems.
We instead stress-tested the *stronger* conjectural bound `n - c`. On the
3-regular circulant `C_n(1, 2)` (frame plus all distance-2 chords) the longest
non-Hamiltonian cycle has length `n - 1` for small `n` (checked `n = 6, 7, 8, 9,
10`), consistent with `c = 1`. On the prism `C_k × K_2` (a 3-regular Hamiltonian
graph on `n = 2k` vertices) the longest non-Hamiltonian cycle also has length
`n - 1`. No 3-regular Hamiltonian example was found whose longest second cycle
falls below `n - O(1)`, matching the Girão–Kittipassorn–Narayanan expectation.

## OEIS

No new integer sequence is introduced; the arc-length identity
`L_forward + L_backward = n + 2` is elementary and needs no lookup.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Long nontrivial cycles in a Hamiltonian graph on `ZMod n`

This file formalizes a fragment of the *long nontrivial cycles conjecture* in the
concrete setting of a Hamiltonian graph whose vertex set is the cyclic group
`ZMod n`.

## Setting

* The vertex type is `V := ZMod n`.
* The *Hamiltonian frame* is the reference Hamiltonian cycle `0 ~ 1 ~ ⋯ ~ (n-1) ~ 0`.
  A pair `{i, j}` is a frame edge when the two vertices are cyclically consecutive,
  i.e. `FrameAdj i j`.
* The ambient graph is an arbitrary `G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)` that *contains* the
  frame (`hframe : ∀ i, G.Adj i (i + 1)`).
* A *chord* is any edge of `G` that is not a frame edge (`IsChord`).
* A *cycle* is an injective cyclic sequence of length `≥ 3`: this is packaged as the
  structure `GraphCycle`, whose vertices are indexed by `ZMod len` so that the
  "wrap-around" adjacency `toFun (len-1) ~ toFun 0` is automatic (it is the case
  `i + 1 = 0` of the `adj` field).
* The reference Hamiltonian cycle itself is `hamiltonianCycle`, which has
  `len = n`.  We record that any cycle of length `< n` is *distinct* from it
  (`second_cycle_ne_hamiltonian`); this is the sense in which the cycles produced
  below are "second cycles".

## Main results

* `chordArcCycle` : every chord `{a, b}` determines a cycle whose length is
  `(b - a).val + 1`, which lies strictly between `2` and `n`.
* `longSecondCycle` : if `G` has minimum degree `≥ 3`, then there is a cycle of
  length `≥ n/2 + 1` that is distinct from the Hamiltonian cycle.
* `everyVertexOnSecondCycle` : under the same hypothesis, every vertex lies on some
  second cycle.

## Proof strategy (no circular dependencies)

The core construction is `arcCycle`: given a starting vertex `a`, a step
`2 ≤ k ≤ n - 2`, and the closing edge `G.Adj (a + k) a`, it walks along the frame
`a, a+1, …, a+k` and then closes up with the given edge.

* `chordArcCycle` feeds a chord `{a, b}` into `arcCycle` with step `k = (b - a).val`.
* `longSecondCycle` extracts a chord from the degree hypothesis, builds the two arc
  cycles for `{a, b}` and `{b, a}` of lengths `k + 1` and `(n - k) + 1`, and keeps
  the longer one (lengths sum to `n + 2`, so the larger is `≥ n/2 + 1`).  This never
  refers to the statement of `longSecondCycle` itself.
* `everyVertexOnSecondCycle` applies `exists_chord_at` at the given vertex `v`.

Strengthen `longSecondCycle` to a sharp `2n/3`-type bound using several chords and
their crossing pattern; drop the cyclic-group indexing in favour of an abstract
Hamiltonian cycle in a general `SimpleGraph`; and analyse how chords may be
combined to lengthen the second cycle beyond a single arc.
-/

namespace LongCycles

/-- The Hamiltonian *frame* adjacency on `ZMod n`: two vertices are frame-adjacent
iff they are cyclically consecutive. -/
def FrameAdj {n : ℕ} (i j : ZMod n) : Prop := j = i + 1 ∨ i = j + 1

/-- A cycle in `G`: an injective cyclic sequence of length `≥ 3`. -/
structure GraphCycle {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)) where
  len : ℕ
  three_le : 3 ≤ len
  toFun : ZMod len → ZMod n
  inj : Function.Injective toFun
  adj : ∀ i : ZMod len, G.Adj (toFun i) (toFun (i + 1))

/-- A *chord* of `G`: an edge of `G` that is not a frame edge. -/
def IsChord {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)) (a b : ZMod n) : Prop :=
  G.Adj a b ∧ ¬ FrameAdj a b

/-- The vertex sequence of the arc cycle starting at `a` with step `k`. -/
def arcToFun {n : ℕ} (a : ZMod n) (k : ℕ) : ZMod (k + 1) → ZMod n :=
  fun j => a + (j.val : ZMod n)

lemma arcToFun_injective {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (a : ZMod n) (k : ℕ) (hkn : k + 1 ≤ n) :
    Function.Injective (arcToFun a k) := by
  intro i j hij
  have h_eq : (i.val : ZMod n) = (j.val : ZMod n) := by
    unfold arcToFun at hij; aesop;
  rw [ ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff ] at h_eq;
  exact ZMod.val_injective _ <| Nat.mod_eq_of_lt ( show i.val < n from lt_of_lt_of_le ( ZMod.val_lt i ) hkn ) ▸ Nat.mod_eq_of_lt ( show j.val < n from lt_of_lt_of_le ( ZMod.val_lt j ) hkn ) ▸ h_eq

lemma arcToFun_adj {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1))
    (a : ZMod n) (k : ℕ) (hkn : k + 2 ≤ n)
    (hclose : G.Adj (a + (k : ZMod n)) a) :
    ∀ i : ZMod (k + 1), G.Adj (arcToFun a k i) (arcToFun a k (i + 1)) := by
  intro i
  by_cases h_m : i.val < k;
  · convert hframe _ using 2;
    unfold arcToFun; norm_num [ ZMod.val_add, h_m ] ;
    erw [ Nat.mod_eq_of_lt ];
    · erw [ ZMod.val_cast_of_lt ] <;> norm_num [ add_assoc ] ; linarith;
    · rcases k with ( _ | _ | k ) <;> simp_all +arith +decide [ ZMod.val ];
  · have h_m_eq : i.val = k := by
      exact le_antisymm ( Nat.le_of_lt_succ i.val_lt ) ( not_lt.mp h_m );
    simp [arcToFun, h_m_eq];
    convert hclose using 1;
    rw [ show i = -1 from by { exact eq_neg_of_add_eq_zero_left <| by { rw [ ← ZMod.natCast_zmod_val i ] ; aesop } } ] ; norm_num

/-- The **arc cycle**: walk along the frame from `a` to `a + k`, then close up. -/
def arcCycle {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1))
    (a : ZMod n) (k : ℕ) (hk2 : 2 ≤ k) (hkn : k + 2 ≤ n)
    (hclose : G.Adj (a + (k : ZMod n)) a) : GraphCycle G where
  len := k + 1
  three_le := by omega
  toFun := arcToFun a k
  inj := arcToFun_injective a k (by omega)
  adj := arcToFun_adj G hframe a k hkn hclose

/-- The reference Hamiltonian cycle, of length `n`. -/
def hamiltonianCycle {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)) (hn : 3 ≤ n)
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1)) : GraphCycle G where
  len := n
  three_le := hn
  toFun := id
  inj := Function.injective_id
  adj := fun i => hframe i

lemma frameAdj_symm {n : ℕ} {a b : ZMod n} (h : FrameAdj a b) : FrameAdj b a := by
  rcases h with h | h
  · exact Or.inr h
  · exact Or.inl h

lemma chord_symm {n : ℕ} {G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)} {a b : ZMod n} (h : IsChord G a b) :
    IsChord G b a := ⟨h.1.symm, fun hf => h.2 (frameAdj_symm hf)⟩

lemma chord_val_bounds {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] {G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n)} {a b : ZMod n}
    (hchord : IsChord G a b) : 2 ≤ (b - a).val ∧ (b - a).val + 2 ≤ n := by
  obtain ⟨h_ne, h_not_frame⟩ := hchord;
  have h_k_ge_2 : (b - a).val ≠ 0 ∧ (b - a).val ≠ 1 ∧ (b - a).val ≠ n - 1 := by
    refine' ⟨ _, _, _ ⟩ <;> intro h_eq <;> simp_all +decide [ FrameAdj ];
    · simp_all +decide [ sub_eq_zero ];
    · rw [ ZMod.val_eq_one ] at h_eq;
      · exact h_not_frame.1 ( by linear_combination' h_eq );
      · contrapose! h_not_frame; interval_cases n <;> simp_all +decide ;
        fin_cases a ; fin_cases b ; trivial;
    · have h_ba_neg_one : b - a = -1 := by
        rcases n with ( _ | _ | n ) <;> simp_all +decide;
        exact ZMod.val_injective _ <| by aesop;
      exact h_not_frame.2 ( by linear_combination' -h_ba_neg_one );
  grind

lemma val_neg_sum {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] {a b : ZMod n} (hab : a ≠ b) :
    (b - a).val + (a - b).val = n := by
  rw [ ← neg_sub, ZMod.neg_val ];
  grind

/-- **Lemma 1 (chordArcCycle).** -/
theorem chordArcCycle {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1)) {a b : ZMod n} (hchord : IsChord G a b) :
    ∃ c : GraphCycle G,
      c.len = (b - a).val + 1 ∧ 2 < c.len ∧ c.len < n ∧ a ∈ Set.range c.toFun := by
  obtain ⟨hk2, hkn⟩ := chord_val_bounds hchord
  have hclose : G.Adj (a + (((b - a).val : ℕ) : ZMod n)) a := by
    have h : a + (((b - a).val : ℕ) : ZMod n) = b := by rw [ZMod.natCast_zmod_val]; ring
    rw [h]; exact hchord.1.symm
  refine ⟨arcCycle G hframe a ((b - a).val) hk2 hkn hclose, rfl, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · show 2 < (b - a).val + 1; omega
  · show (b - a).val + 1 < n; omega
  · exact ⟨0, by simp [arcCycle, arcToFun]⟩

    (hdeg : ∀ v : ZMod n, 3 ≤ (G.neighborSet v).ncard) (v : ZMod n) :
    ∃ w : ZMod n, IsChord G v w := by
  by_contra! h;
  have h_subset : G.neighborSet v ⊆ {v + 1, v - 1} := by
    intro w hw; specialize h w; simp_all +decide [ IsChord ] ;
    cases h <;> simp_all +decide [ eq_sub_iff_add_eq ];
  exact absurd ( Set.ncard_le_ncard h_subset ) ( by have := hdeg v; exact not_le_of_gt ( lt_of_le_of_lt ( Set.ncard_insert_le _ _ ) ( by norm_num; linarith ) ) ) ;

/-- **Lemma 2 (longSecondCycle).** -/
theorem longSecondCycle {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1))
    (hdeg : ∀ v : ZMod n, 3 ≤ (G.neighborSet v).ncard) :
    ∃ c : GraphCycle G, n / 2 + 1 ≤ c.len ∧ c.len < n := by
  obtain ⟨b, hchord⟩ := exists_chord_at hdeg 0
  obtain ⟨c1, hlen1, _, hlt1, _⟩ := chordArcCycle G hframe hchord

  have hne : (0 : ZMod n) ≠ b := fun h => (hchord.1.ne) h

  by_cases h : n / 2 + 1 ≤ c1.len
  · exact ⟨c1, h, hlt1⟩
  · exact ⟨c2, by omega, hlt2⟩

/-- **Lemma 3 (everyVertexOnSecondCycle).** -/
theorem everyVertexOnSecondCycle {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (G : SimpleGraph (ZMod n))
    (hframe : ∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj i (i + 1))
    (hdeg : ∀ v : ZMod n, 3 ≤ (G.neighborSet v).ncard) (v : ZMod n) :
    ∃ c : GraphCycle G, 2 < c.len ∧ c.len < n ∧ v ∈ Set.range c.toFun := by
  obtain ⟨w, hchord⟩ := exists_chord_at hdeg v
  obtain ⟨c, _, h2, hlt, hmem⟩ := chordArcCycle G hframe hchord

# Future Directions: Long Nontrivial Cycles in Hamiltonian Graphs

This cycle established that a single chord in a Hamiltonian graph of minimum
degree three forces a second cycle of length exactly half the perimeter,
uniformly across all vertices, and that this half-perimeter guarantee is the best
obtainable from one chord alone. The gap to the conjectural `n - c` therefore
lives entirely in the *interaction* between several chords. The following
conjectures are framed to attack that gap.

## Conjecture 1 (Two crossing chords already beat the half bound)

If a Hamiltonian graph of minimum degree three contains two chords that *cross*
(their endpoints alternate around the frame), then it contains a second cycle of
length at least `2n/3`.

The key insight is that two crossing chords partition the frame into four arcs,
and one can route a single cycle through three of the four arcs — discarding only
the shortest — instead of being confined to one arc as with a lone chord.

Why now? The single-chord analysis shows the half bound is *tight* precisely
because only one arc is used; crossing is the minimal structural feature that
lets a cycle re-use more than one arc, so it is the natural first step beyond the
half bound and is entirely combinatorial.

## Conjecture 2 (Chord density forces near-Hamiltonian second cycles)

If a Hamiltonian graph on `n` vertices has at least `n` chords (equivalently,
average degree at least four on top of the frame), then it contains a second
cycle of length at least `n - O(log n)`.

The key insight is that with linearly many chords the "short arcs" they cut off
can be individually bypassed, and a bypassed arc removes only its own length from
the achievable cycle, so plentiful short chords erode the deficit logarithmically
rather than polynomially.

Why now? Minimum degree three yields at least `n/2` chords by an elementary
degree count; doubling that count to `n` is a modest strengthening under which
the deficit's dependence on `n` should provably collapse, isolating where the
polynomial error bounds in the general problem come from.

## Conjecture 3 (Bounded chord span is the only obstruction)

A Hamiltonian graph of minimum degree three fails to contain a second cycle of
length `n - c` (for the optimal absolute `c`) only if all but `c` of its chords
have span (cyclic distance) bounded by an absolute constant.

The key insight is that a long-span chord contributes a long arc directly, so the
extremal graphs for the conjecture must hide all their length in many short-span
chords clustered near the frame, turning the problem into one about local chord
patterns rather than global structure.

Why now? The proved arc-length identity `L_forward + L_backward = n + 2` shows a
single long-span chord already gives a long cycle, so the extremal analysis can
be reduced to short-span chords — a finite, checkable local configuration space.

## Conjecture 4 (Vertex-uniform strengthening)

In a Hamiltonian graph of minimum degree three, *every* vertex lies on a second
cycle of length at least `n - c` for an absolute constant `c`, not merely some
vertex.

The key insight is that the half-perimeter guarantee is already vertex-uniform,
so the correct strong form of the conjecture should be uniform as well: the
extremal length bound ought not to depend on which vertex one insists the long
cycle pass through.

Why now? The uniform half bound (every vertex sits on a nontrivial cycle) is now
established, making the uniform version of the full conjecture a precise and
natural target rather than a vague hope, and offering a stronger induction
hypothesis for attacking the existential version.

concept.concept_description: The shadowing lemma says that near an approximate orbit of a chaotic system, there exists a true orbit. In other words, every 'almost correct' trajectory of a chaotic map has a 'truly correct' trajectory nearby. Impact: numerical chaos is not error — it is a computable shadow of mathematical truth. Your computer's rounding errors are tracing out REAL orbits of the chaotic system.
